hero.name: Ishita
hero.who: a 19-year-old fine arts student in Kolkata who thinks every good idea is taken

story.b: Ishita is in her first year of fine arts in Kolkata. She wants to make comics, but every time she has an idea, she finds it online already. A girl in Mumbai draws city comics. A boy in Bengaluru draws food comics. A studio in Delhi makes folk-style animation. Each time, Ishita closes her sketchbook and feels like a copy. Her notebook is full of half-finished first pages. Her classmates post their work every week, while she posts nothing. One evening, on the tram back from College Street, she scrolls past yet another artist doing exactly what she had imagined. She decides, again, that there is no point. Everything good has already been done.

ask.q: Ishita keeps quitting because her ideas seem taken. What would help her most?
o: Stop looking at anyone's work so nothing influences her
Wait for a completely original idea nobody has ever had
Learn openly from many artists she admires and blend them into her own work
ask.why: Avoiding all influence leaves her with nothing to build from, and a completely original idea may never come. Every creator builds on others. Studying many influences openly and transforming them is how a personal voice is actually found.

chapters.take: Every new idea is built from older ones. Start anyway.

story.b: Ishita lists five creators she admires and one thing each does brilliantly. The old Kalighat painters, for their bold, flowing lines. Japanese comics, for the way their panels move. Her grandmother's kantha embroidery, for its patient patterns. The hand-painted signboards in her para, for their bright lettering. A Bengali children's magazine from her mother's childhood, for its gentle humour. She studies each closely, then tries drawing one page that mixes all five. It looks strange at first. By the third try, it looks like nothing she has seen before. In the margin, she writes down her influences, giving them credit. It feels honest, and for the first time, it feels like hers.

ask.q: Ishita's classmate loves one famous illustrator and copies her style exactly. What advice fits best?
o: Study many artists deeply, credit them and blend them into something new
Keep copying that one artist, since her style is proven
Avoid looking at any artist so she stays original
ask.why: Copying one artist is imitation, and avoiding everyone leaves nothing to build on. Studying many sources, giving credit and transforming what she learns turns borrowing into originality, because the blend becomes her own.

chapters.take: Copy one and you imitate. Blend many and you create.

story.b: Ishita starts collecting everything that sparks an idea. A torn tram ticket with a lovely font. A photo of a tea stall's chalkboard menu. A funny line overheard on a crowded bus. A tune her father hums while cooking fish curry. She keeps them in a shoebox and a notes folder on her phone. Then she gets curious about the comic artist she loves most and reads about who inspired him. That leads her to an old newspaper cartoonist, and from there to a printmaker she had never heard of. Each step opens another door. Her shoebox grows heavy, and her sketchbook no longer runs dry when she sits down to draw.

ask.q: Ishita's friend says she has no ideas when she sits down to draw. What would help her most?
o: Wait for inspiration to arrive on its own
Keep a collection of things that spark her, and trace who inspired her heroes
Look only at the most popular artists online
ask.why: Waiting for inspiration often means waiting forever, and popular artists alone offer a narrow view. Collecting what sparks her and following the chain of who inspired her heroes builds a rich store of ideas to draw from.

chapters.take: Collect what sparks you, and follow your heroes back to their heroes.

story.b: One Saturday, Ishita watches the girls in her para play football in the lane outside the sweet shop, shouting and laughing. She realises she has never seen a comic about girls like them, in a Kolkata para, with kantha patterns and painted signboards in the background. She searches online and finds nothing quite like it. That empty space feels like an invitation. She stops worrying about what her style is and simply starts drawing the comic she wishes someone else had already made. The first chapter is clumsy. But page after page, her lines grow more confident, and her own style starts to show itself, discovered through the work.

ask.q: Ishita's classmate wants to figure out her artistic identity before starting any project. What should Ishita suggest?
o: Make the thing she wishes existed, and discover her style by doing it
Read more about art theory until her style becomes clear
Copy trending projects until she finds what works
ask.why: Thinking endlessly about identity delays the work that would reveal it, and trending copies lead away from her own voice. Making the thing she wishes existed gives her a reason to start, and her style appears through the making.

chapters.take: Make the thing you wish existed. Your style shows up as you work.

story.b: Halfway through, Ishita gets stuck. She has been drawing on her tablet for weeks, undoing every line, and the pages feel stiff. One evening she pushes the tablet aside and spreads old newspapers on the floor. She cuts out shapes, glues them down, splashes watercolour and sticks notes with ideas all over the wall. Her hands get messy, and she feels like a child again. She also starts a side project just for fun: painting a new signboard for her friend's tea stall near the bus stop. While mixing paints for the sign, she suddenly sees how to draw the big match scene. The idea came from her hands, not her screen.

ask.q: Ishita's friend has been stuck staring at her laptop for hours. What should she try?
o: Stay at the laptop until the idea finally comes
Watch more tutorials on the same screen
Step away and make something by hand, like sketching or cutting paper
ask.why: Staring longer at the same screen often deepens the block, and more tutorials keep her stuck in the same place. Working with her hands and playing with side projects brings her body into it and often sparks ideas a screen alone cannot.

chapters.take: Get your hands involved. Ideas often come away from the screen.

story.b: Ishita used to work in wild bursts, drawing all night and then doing nothing for a week. Now she keeps a simple routine. She sleeps by midnight, draws for two hours each morning before classes and keeps a small budget for her pocket money so money worries do not distract her. Every Sunday, she shares one finished page online, with a short note about her process. A few people follow. Some leave kind comments. One stranger writes something nasty about her drawing. Ishita reads it once, does not reply and spends her energy praising other young artists instead. A small comics group in Shillong finds her through those comments and invites her to collaborate.

ask.q: Ishita gets a cruel comment on a page she shared. What should she do?
o: Delete all her work and stop sharing
Ignore the troll, keep sharing steadily and stay generous to others
ask.why: Deleting her work lets one stranger decide her path, and an angry reply only feeds the troll. Ignoring it, sharing small pieces regularly and being generous to other artists keeps her energy on the work and helps the right people find her.

chapters.take: A steady routine and generous sharing beat rare bursts of genius.

story.h: A comic at the college fest
story.b: Weeks later, at the college fest, Ishita sits behind a small table with forty printed copies of her comic about the para football girls. The cover has bold Kalighat lines, panels that move like the Japanese comics she loves and kantha borders around the edges. On the back page, she lists her influences. By evening, every copy is gone. A first-year student asks her how she found her style. Ishita laughs and says she found it by making things, not by waiting. The girls from her para come to the stall and see themselves in the drawings. One of them demands a bigger role in the next chapter. Ishita has already started drawing it.

chapters.take: Learn from many, make what you wish existed, and keep showing up.
